ROLEX SUBMARINER DATE 1680 MK2
movement: AUTOMATIC Rolex released the ref. 1680 in 1967 as the original "Date Sub," more than a decade after the Submariner’s inception. It features a distinctly different case design and a unique “Top Hat” crystal with the iconic cyclops magnifier. In the first decade of its life, these watches were affectionately known as “Red Subs” due to the distinctive red lettering on their dials. Over time, the Red Sub has become one of the most sought-after vintage Rolex models—a "grail" for many collectors, with a price tag to match. In comparison, the "White" 1680s are perhaps some of the most under-appreciated vintage Rolexes. Produced between 1976 and 1979, they feature white text across three dial variants—commonly referred to as the Mk1, Mk2, and Mk3 white dials. The current example from 1979 sports a Mk2 dial in superb condition. The tritium lume on the markers and hands has aged to a rich, creamy hue, and the dial remains free of imperfections. The case has been polished in the past but remains strong—especially the lugs. The original Mk3 insert has faded to a striking blue colour, offering amazing contrast to the dial. The original silver date wheel is still present, and the full-link 93150 bracelet shows minimal stretch, the clasp is a service replacement from 1995. The watch comes with its original wallet with serial sticker and translation papers. The movement runs beautifully at +3 s/d, 295 amplitude, with a 0.4 ms beat error—an honest example of a Rolex icon

ref: ROLEX AIR KING 5500
movement: AUTOMATIC After hearing stories of British pilots discarding their standard-issue field watches in favour of personally purchased Oyster Perpetuals, Rolex co-founder Hans Wilsdorf decided to release a series of aviation-themed watches honouring the RAF pilots who flew in the Battle of Britain. Among them was the Air-King, which made its first official appearance in 1945 with reference 4925. Several references followed as Rolex refined the design, before introducing the reference 5500 in 1957, officially sold to the public from 1958. By modern standards, the 5500 may seem small and understated for a steel Rolex, but what it lacks in size it makes up for in stamina. It holds the distinction of being the longest-running model in Rolex history, remaining in continuous production from 1957 to 1989. Over those 32 years, remarkably little changed. Apart from a movement upgrade in 1963 and the edition of the Explorer dials, much of it stayed the same. The example from 68 has survived well, the soleil grey dial is in beautiful condition with all of its lume plots intact, the same goes for the hands. The case has been subject to very little polishing, the watch did have its original bracelet but it had sadly perished. The previous owner had the Rolex buckle and strap fitted at St James's last year. The watch has just been serviced and is running beautifully at +6 s/d, 265 amps and has a beat error of 0.1ms

ref: ROLEX EXPLORER 36 114270 ‘FULL SET’
movement: AUTOMATIC The Rolex Explorer 114270 unveiled in 2001, taking over from the 14270 after twelve years of service. Compared to the transition from 1016 to 14270, Rolex didn't change a whole lot this time. Why would it? - it's difficult to improve something that was already close to perfect. The movement was upgraded to the Cal. 3130 and solid end links were added. This example is from 2008 and retains its original full link bracelet and clasp stamped PJ12 (Dec 08). The watch is in great condition; the case is super sharp and the lugs are even. The sapphire glass is unmarked. It was serviced by Rolex in 2024. The watch is running perfectly, at +2 s/d, 285 amps, and 0.1 ms beat error. It comes with its full set; both tags, booklets, wallet, calendar, inner and outer boxes, and the original guarantee. In a world full of oversized modern watches, this is the perfect antidote, a jack of all trades too

ref: LEMANIA WWW DIRTY DOZEN 'PROMETHIUM DIAL'
movement: MANUAL WIND Few military watches have achieved the legendary status of the “Dirty Dozen” WWW watches. Commissioned by the Ministry of Defence during the Second World War, twelve Swiss manufacturers were tasked with producing robust, accurate and highly legible wristwatches capable of withstanding the demands of active service. The result was a distinctive group of timepieces united by their utilitarian design, black dials, luminous Arabic numerals, subsidiary seconds and the iconic WWW — “Watch, Wrist, Waterproof” — marking on the dial. The Dirty Dozen is particularly fascinating because each manufacturer interpreted the brief in its own way, creating subtle differences in cases, dials, movements and finishing. The Lemania we have here is part of that twelve but with an interesting twist, it has a Promethium dial. In the 60's when the regulations around radioactive material were increasing, the MOD and watchmakers had to take note and start using different luminescent material on their dials. Tritium was the preferred material but Promethium was also used. Known for its super bright glow, they used this material right up to the 90's. Its half life of 2.5 years meant it needed reluming often or have dials swopped to make sure it continued to glow. movement: AUTOMATIC The Omega Seamaster 300 began its life in 1957 with Ref. CK2913, launched alongside the Speedmaster and Railmaster to form the “Master Trilogy.” Although the Seamaster name dates back to the 1940s, the SM300 was the first true diver’s watch Omega produced, with a guaranteed water resistance of 200m (tested to 300m, hence the name). Early SM300s, such as the CK2913 and CK14755, feature a straight-lug case (38–39mm) and thin bezels. In 1963, Omega introduced an entirely redesigned SM300 line, marking the start of the “Lyre Lugs” era. Made between 1963 and 1971, the new SM300 features a larger case accommodating a wider, thicker, and far more legible bezel with distinct clicks during rotation. The dials also gained larger index markers and hands. Ref. ST 165.024 (no date) and ref. ST 166.024 (date) represent what many consider the most successful Seamaster design—state-of-the-art divers in their day and some of the most enjoyable Omegas to collect, thanks to numerous variations produced over a relatively short period. At first glance, the watch we have for sale here is an early and very honest 165.024, with its original gilt-print dial, “Type B” straight hands, original small-logo crystal, and a superbly strong case. However, one immediately notices that the tritium acrylic insert has aged to a rich blue hue instead of the expected black. Once thought to be a manufacturing defect or even counterfeit, Omega collectors eventually reached a consensus that the blue insert is indeed original. All known examples share the same insert type, including the distinctive slanted 3 in “30.” As of 2020/2021, only nine “Blueberry” examples have been documented. You can imagine our excitement when we carefully removed the mud and dirt from this watch after it arrived, having spent decades in a drawer. The dial is spotless, as is the insert. ref: ROLEX GMT MASTER 16753 'NIPPLE DIAL'
movement: AUTOMATIC The 16753, affectionately known among collectors as the “Root Beer” due to its distinctive bezel colours, was introduced in the late 1970s as the second generation of the bi-metal GMT-Master, succeeding the 1675/3. This model came in two variations: the traditional Root Beer with a brown dial and bi-colour bezel, and this particular variant featuring a black dial with an all-black bezel. As a transitional model alongside the 16750, the 16753 featured the automatic calibre 3075, offering a quickset date and a higher beat rate—both upgrades from the 1675/3. The watch is also notable for another distinctive feature: the “Nipple Dial,” named for the unique gold hour markers that protrude slightly from the surface. The tritium hands have aged to a subtle off-white, as have the tops of the nipple markers. The open 6 and 9 date wheel has developed a pleasing patina. The case remains unpolished. The G (82)-stamped 78363/480 Oyster bracelet is one link short and exhibits minimal sag. The movement has recently been serviced and is running at +3 seconds per day, with an amplitude of 275 and a beat error of 0.2

ref: A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Blue Dial - Box and Papers (Ref. 206.027)
model_name: a rich blue dial with applied white gold markers and subsidiary seconds at six. Turn it over, and the personality changes completely. The exhibition caseback reveals the manually wound Lange movement, where the restrained design of the dial gives way to the elaborate finishing for which the manufacture became famous. The broad German silver three-quarter plate, heat-blued screws, gold chatons, and hand-finished components make the back of the watch every bit as interesting as the front. It is one of the reasons early and understated Lange watches have become so compelling to collectors. The complexity isn't there to attract attention from across the room. It is there for the owner. The reference 206.027 captures what A. Lange & Söhne does exceptionally well. It looks simple until you begin paying attention. Writer's Thoughts White gold and blue might be the best combination for a 1815. From the wrist, this A. Lange & Söhne is incredibly restrained. The white metal case doesn't announce itself as precious metal, while the blue dial gives the watch enough color to keep it from becoming overly formal. That contrast is really the entire appeal. The front is almost austere, while the movement is filled with the kind of tiny finishing details you can spend an unreasonable amount of time examining. The display caseback isn't an afterthought on a Lange. It is a major reason you buy one. This example retains its original strap and buckle and is accompanied by its box and papers, making an already desirable 1815 configuration considerably more complete.
